title: Pulmonary System • Core Concepts (Advanced)
source_note: Generalized from teaching notes; curated for advanced proficiency; no copyrighted verbatim.

items.question: A right mainstem aspiration is more common during blind ETT advancement primarily because the right bronchus is:
options: Shorter, more vertical, and wider than the left
Longer, more horizontal, and narrower than the left
Supported by fewer cartilage rings than the left
Innervated differently by the phrenic nerve
items.rationale: Right main bronchus: shallower angle (~25°), wider, shorter → inadvertent intubation/aspiration risk.
items.clinical_pearl: Unilateral breath sounds after ETT advancement: withdraw 1–2 cm and reassess.

items.question: Stimulation at the carina during suctioning can precipitate bradycardia and hypotension due to:
options: Vagal reflex activation from rich parasympathetic fibers
Direct suppression of SA node automaticity by hypoxia alone
items.rationale: Carina is vagally rich; mechanical stimulation triggers parasympathetic response.

items.question: Type II pneumocytes primarily:
options: Produce/recycle surfactant and can differentiate after injury
Form tight junctions impermeable to water under normal states
items.rationale: Type II cells synthesize surfactant and proliferate after type I injury.
items.clinical_pearl: Surfactant loss → ↑ surface tension → atelectasis → ↓ compliance.

items.question: Loss of negative intrapleural pressure results in immediate alveolar collapse because:
options: Alveolar elastic recoil exceeds transmural distending pressure
Bronchial circulation shunts blood to the pleura
items.rationale: Without negative pleural pressure, distending pressure falls and elastic recoil collapses alveoli (e.g., pneumothorax).

items.question: Movement from normal to markedly high V/Q in a lung unit most likely occurs with:
items.rationale: PE decreases perfusion with preserved ventilation → high V/Q (dead space).
items.clinical_pearl: High V/Q = wasted ventilation; Low V/Q = shunt-like.

items.question: Clinically significant shunt is suspected when PaO2 remains <60 mm Hg despite:
options: Lowering plateau pressure below 20 cm H2O
items.rationale: Failure to correct hypoxemia with moderate-to-high FiO2 suggests shunt physiology (e.g., ARDS).

items.question: In the upright patient, accurate PAOP measurements require the catheter tip be in:
items.rationale: Only zone 3 reliably reflects left atrial pressure: Pa > Pv > PA.

items.question: On mechanical ventilation, a progressive rise in peak pressure with stable plateau pressure most strongly indicates:
items.rationale: Peak–plateau gap widens with resistance (bronchospasm, secretions).
items.clinical_pearl: Rising plateau implies compliance problem (edema, ARDS).

items.question: Which intervention increases alveolar driving pressure for O2 diffusion without directly changing FiO2?
options: Raise tidal volume from 6 to 10 ml/kg
items.rationale: PEEP/CPAP elevates mean airway pressure and maintains alveolar patency.

items.question: Which positioning best improves oxygenation in right-sided pneumonia?
items.rationale: Good-lung-down maximizes V/Q matching.

items.question: A leftward shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve will most likely:
options: Impair O2 loading in the lungs
Improve loading in lungs but hinder unloading in tissues
Have no effect on O2 affinity
items.rationale: Left shift increases affinity—easier pickup, tougher delivery (alkalosis, hypothermia, ↓2,3‑DPG).

items.question: Banked PRBC transfusions can transiently reduce tissue O2 delivery because of:
options: High dissolved O2 in the unit
items.rationale: Stored blood has low 2,3‑DPG → greater Hb–O2 affinity → reduced tissue unloading.

items.question: Which intervention increases CaO2 most effectively?
options: Raise FiO2 from 0.5 to 0.8 in severe anemia (Hgb 6 g/dl)
Transfuse to raise Hgb with adequate saturation
Small increase in PaO2 from 80 to 120 mm Hg
items.rationale: O2 content ~ Hgb × 1.34 × SaO2; dissolved O2 is minor.

items.question: The Haldane effect explains:
options: Why hypoventilation causes hypercapnia before hypoxemia
How oxygenation of Hb in the lungs promotes CO2 unloading
How acidosis raises affinity for O2
Why CO2 diffuses 20× slower than O2
items.rationale: Oxygenation reduces Hb affinity for CO2, facilitating CO2 release; deoxygenation allows CO2 uptake.

items.question: Which scenario most likely increases O2 unloading at tissues (right shift)?
options: Sepsis with fever and lactic acidosis
items.rationale: Acidemia/hyperthermia shift right.

items.question: A volume-control patient shows rising plateau and peak pressures, falling compliance, and hypoxemia refractory to FiO2 0.6. Most consistent physiology is:
options: Shunt physiology such as diffuse atelectasis/ARDS
items.rationale: Refractory hypoxemia with low compliance points to shunt physiology (e.g., ARDS).

items.question: High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) improves oxygenation by all EXCEPT:
items.rationale: HFNC aids oxygenation/ventilation mechanics but does not change hemoglobin.

items.question: PEEP titration that reduces driving pressure (plateau − PEEP) while maintaining PaO2 ≥60 mm Hg suggests:
items.rationale: Lower driving pressure correlates with improved outcomes.

items.question: During severe asthma, which ventilator change best addresses dynamic hyperinflation?
options: Decrease rate and prolong expiratory time (lower minute ventilation target)
items.rationale: Allow more time for exhalation to reduce air trapping; avoid high VT.

items.question: Kerley B lines on CXR most directly reflect:
options: Thickened interlobular septa from interstitial edema and lymphatic engorgement
items.rationale: Kerley B lines = interstitial edema with lymphatic congestion.
